newsitem.title: CHINA: Shangri-La Asia says new hotels, charges trim gains.
newsitem.headline: Shangri-La Asia says new hotels, charges trim gains.

text.p: Shangri-La Asia Ltd posted a 6.3 percent decline in net profit for the first six months of the year on Wednesday, hit by start-up losses at its three new hotels in China and higher charges.

The hotel arm of Malaysia's Kuok Group said net profit fell to HK$470.95 million compared with HK$502.48 million in the same period last year. Turnover rose to HK$1.64 billion compared with HK$1.40 billion in the first six months of 1996.

"The decline in attributable profits was due to increased interest expense, higher taxation charges and start-up losses of the three new hotels in China which opened in 1996," Shangri-La Asia said in a statement.
But the Asian hotel owner was still optimistic about profits for the whole year in 1997.

"It is anticipated that in the high season we will show growth so we are still very optmistic that for the full year we will gain occupancy levels," managing director Paul Bush told a news conference on the interim results.

Shangri-La Asia also announced a HK$1.2 billion deal to buy 100 percent of hotel management and marketing company SLIM International Ltd from the Kuok Group through the issue of 135.9 million new shares to its parent at HK$8.83 a share.
This compared with the stock's last close of HK$8.80 per share on Tuesday before trading was suspended on Wednesday, pending the announcement.
The deal would lift the Kuok Group's interest in Shangri-La Asia to 62.2 percent from 58.9 percent, Bush said.

SLIM International is the holding company of the hotel management and marketing subsidiaries of the Shangri-La group, known as Shangri-La Hotels and Resorts. It manages hotels and resorts principally owned by Shangri-La Asia and other members of the Kuok Group as well as third party owners.
Through SLIM International, Shangri-La Asia said it would have 35 hotels under management after the transaction.
Following the acquisition of SLIM, the group would be able to consider the possibility of managing hotels outside the East Asian area, Bush said.
Contributions from Shangri-La Asia's Beijing hotels declined during the six months to June 30 due to slower demand from business travellers, the company said.
Consolidated operating profit, excluding the three new hotels opened in 1996, fell five percent to HK$91 million while the three new hotels posted an operating loss of HK$37 million.
But Shangri-La Asia said as economic fundamentals in China continued to improve, business travel should rise.
Shangri-La Asia said operating profit from its Hong Kong hotels rose by nine percent to HK$259 million.
It said demand for rooms had softened from May to August, except for the period straddling Hong Kong's July 1 return to Chinese rule, due to slower demand from Japan.

Shangri-La Asia said operating profit from its Philippines hotels rose by 22 percent to HK$169 million. Its three hotels achieved a steady combined average occupancy rate of 82 percent and combined average room rates rose 11 percent to HK$1,260.
Its two Fiji hotels saw operating profit rise to HK$18 million from HK$6 million and while the contribution from the Shangri-La hotel in Jakarta fell to HK$4 million from HK$7 million last year.
